title: Lecture 8-31-2026
text:
Reference Notes

State, Sovereignty
There is no higher power above the state within it’s own territory. Each state should be allowed to dictate it’s own behavior. No international actor should be allowed to dictate a state’s behavior. This is the concept of Sovereignty.
Anarchy is the absecene of supra-national authority. There is no enforcement mechanism other than the soverignty of the state.
The treaty of Westphalia (1648) is considered as the reference point for the idea of the modern state or when state sovereignty was first recognized.
A State is a formal legal system with a central authority that makes and enforces it rules within a defined territory.
A nation is a cultural group of people and it not recognized as an international actor.
Nation-State is a state that shares within itself a unified social and cultural identity.
Country is a common term to refer to a geographic area of a state.
Extra-Systemic Conflict: When a state fights against a non-state actor.

US achieved internal sovreighty by declaring itself indepdent in 1776, but it lacked external sovreighty (it wasn’t recognized by external states). But in 1781 when the Treaty of Paris was signed the US gained external sovreighty.
Autonomous Territories look like states but are not actually states, e.g. Greenland.

title: Lecture 9-14-2026
text:
Democracies are not inherently more peacful towards autocracies.
Democracies tend to be more peaceful towards other democracies. However, democracies are as likely as autocracies to initate interstate conflicts.
Diatic Democratic Peace: Democracies are more peacful to eachother but just as violent as other political systems when not dealing with other democracies.


Democratic norms tend to have less human rights violations, and they tend to be lesser in severity when compared to autocracy. Autocracies are more likely to use violence to resolve domestic disputes.
Key Assumptions*

Externalization:
Institutionalization: Selectorate Theory - The fundamental difference between autocratic and democractic societies is the size of winning coalition. When multiple people have a say in domestic politics are called the selectorate. The support of the selectorate for a leader is not necessary for their political survival, for example you want people to support your party when you exit office so they will elect your party. The same applies to autocracies, in fact it’s more severe there because their literal survival is on the line if they lose power.

In order for leaders to accomplish their survival they must understand whose support is necessary for survival. Support of the entire selectorate tends to not be neccesary, the members whose support is necessary for the survival of the leader is considered the “winning coalition”. For example in an autocracy this “winning coalition” might be just the military leadership, etc.
In a democracy the winning coalition tends to be much larger than that of the winning coalition in an autocracy. In a democractic society the winning coalition tends to be broad public support.
Autocratic leaders tend to use private goods to entice military leadership to support their regime. Private goods are like patronage goods, they are given only to a small group of peoples.
In democratic societies, leaders tend to win broad public support (or support of their winning coalition) via the provision to the general public of public goods. Public goods tend to be more effecient at capturing winning coalition than private goods because it can grab larger support than the scarce private goods.
Assumption War Outcomes are a public good. Meaning a democratic leader must win active wars in order to survive as a leader. Therefore, democratic leaders tend to be very cautious in selecting when to engage in wars, and when they do engage in war they tend to select easier opponents to ensure positive outcomes in wartime. In autocracies, leaders have a lesser incentive to see positive outcomes in wars and therefore autocracies tend to have more wreckless foreign policy.

However this outcome could be argued to be wrong because in a democratic society the outcome of a war tends not to benefit the totality of the winning coalition, instead it behaves more like a private good because it benefits a select few while still imposing costs on the broad public.


Constraints Persepective: Regardless of regime type, many people do not want to pay the huge cost of war. Democratic leaders have to pay more attention to public support/aversion to any given conflict. This plays heavily into their decision to decide to fight a war or not.
Democracies are more transparent than autocracies. Information is more freely available in democracies. Economic data published by China is less trusworthy. War and conflict is more likely when there is large uncertainty. When democracies are in crisis there tends to be less uncertainty, which means less conflict. Democracies have more informational advantages which means they are more certain and therefore much less likely to engage in conflict. When democracies make threats therefore, they tend to be more credible. When democratic leaders make a public announcement or a threat, it is politically costly, this is called audience talk, because the threat ties to democratic leaders hands with his winning coalition, the democratic leaders more likely to follow through because he will pay a much higher political cost. If the democratic leader doesn’t follow through he pays a high audience cost.
Democratic citizens do not want to fight against other democracies. Democratic public opinion has a strong sway on democratic leaders to prevent war against other democracies.
Socialization: If you are brought up in a system where it is not normal to use force or violence against opposition, you will tend not to use, the same could be inversely said about those raised under autocratic systems. This explanations shortcoming is that it points more to a monotonic democratic peace, but this peace lacks empirical evidence.

Copeland’s Trade Exepctation Theory: High current interdependence, with a positive outlook on the future -> This leads to further peace. Whereas, with high current interdependence and a negative outlook for the future, war becomes MORE likely. The direction of expectations matters more than the level of trade itself.
Examples of Copelan’s theory: Germany (1914, 1939), Japan (1941), Russian/Ukraine(2022).
Opium Wars:
In the 1700’s the British had a high demand for Chinese Tea, China wanted virtually nothing in return for tea but British paid them in Silver. The British East India Company grew opium in India and smuggled it into China, eve tually the trade balance flipped and China was paying Britian instead.
Opdium addicition spread so severely that in 1839 Qing official Lin Zexu confiscated and destroyed over 20,000 chests of British Opium in Canton effectively banning the trade.
There were two Opium wars that followed.
The War of 1812:
During the Napoleonic Wars, the British issued the ‘Orders in Council’ blockading French ports and seizing neutral American ships trading with France.
British warships practiced impressement stopping American vessels and forcibly conscripting American sailors into the British navy.
President Madison and Congress conlfuded that trade depdence on Britian had become a tool of coercian not a source of mutual retstraint.

title: Lecture 8-28-2026
text:
Rival States vs Non-Rival States

In Rival States, population aging is negatively associated with military spending
In Rival States population aging is negatively associated with armed forces personnel counts
In Non-Rival States with an aging population, with an already low level of military spending, the same cuts have further negative effects on military spending and lack of external threats mean that these states spend the minimum they can on their military.








Note



When testing these hypotheses it’s important to find the variables for \(x\) and \(y\) where \(x\) is commonly referred to as the independent variable or explanatory variable. Whereas \(y\) is commonly referred to as the dependant variable, the outcome, or the response variable.


In our Hypotheses we have 3 variables:

Population age, military spending, and rivalry status.

Another variable \(z\) is considered our moderating variable (or condition), this reveals that the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) differs based on the presence of \(z\).


In this step of research, we want to find empirical patterns in our associations to see if our hypotheses is correct.
While doing this you have to consider:

Sample Size (In this hypotheses all countries between 1970-2015)

Spacial: Which countries do you select (all African countries?)
Temporal: What historical period (Post cold war, pre cold war, pre world war 2?)

Unit of Analysis

USA from 1975 -> 2015
China from 1975 -> 2015
Military personnel per 1000 people.

One reason to choose this amount is because countries have a variable population size and therefore comparing purely active personnel as a total count is not a fair comparison to how aggressively a country is staffing it’s military.


Estimator

A statistical platform in which estimate the association between x and y.
If our outcome variable is continuous, binary, dichotamous, ordinal, nominal, event count.

Systematic:

Why does military spending change as a result of our other variables?

Random Noise

Effectively we want to ignore random noise that affects our variables but do not have anything to do with our hypothesus.

Ordinal: 5 multiple choices with an order.
These are ways to do statistical models.







Note



For our final paper we’re going to want to inlcude our Operationalization and our Sample.

title: Lecture 9-18-2026
text:
Democracy
Ecnonomic Interdependance
International Institutions

Neoliberal institutionalists focus more on the roles of International Institutions in their effectiveness in guarding peace amongst liberal societies. They believe that because International Institutions reduce uncertainty, and because uncertainty increases the probability of conflict, the reduction causes by International Institutions is more effective therefore at keeping the peace.
International Institutions also reduce transactions costs. So during crisis negotiations because two states have experience negotiating through the international institutions negotiations tend to go smoother. International Institutions can also hold states accountable by providing punitive restrictions. International Institutions can also provide dispute resolution, for example arbitration through the WTO for countries that have trade conflict.




Slightly different version of Liberal Peace. When countries have financial independence they tend to remain peaceful with eachother.
The more trade between states the more peaceful those states tend to be with eachother.
Tying Hands and Sunk Cost mechanism:
If you tie your hands and make your threat credible. If I have spent too much money (sunk cost) and my hands are tied my threat is much more credible.
When a country is much more dependent on one country then when the less dependent country makes a threat it can be viewed as credible. This will lead to a higher probability of a negotiated peace or policy change.
However, the empirical finding of this situation is mixed.



Trade reduces conflict is the hypothesus, however, there is not an empirical finding that clearly backs that idea.
First, how do you measure trade dependence? - Weak Link Measure: Between State 1 and State 2, given the total trade volume between the two states divided by GDP for both countries:
$$
\frac{\text{Total Trade Volume}}{\text{GDP}_1} \lt \frac{\text{Total Trade Volume}}{\text{GDP}_2}
$$

Therefore, State 1 is the weak link because less of it's GDP comes with the trade from State 1. While State 1 may have more resources to fight, it can avoid conflict by just trading which makes it less likely to initiate conflict. 

Salience Symmetry: When neither state is particularly dependent or both are equally dependent conflict is less likely overall.
Endogeneity: Since we cannot clearly say that trade prevents or causes conflict and vice versa, Endogenity argues that with a high probability of conflict trade will reduce. Because both trade and coflict have a negative correlation with eachother, reduced trade as a result of conlfict is a side effect of conflict not a cause of it.

What instruments are good predictors of trade? These are Endogenous factors, they do not cause or are not caused by conflict but because of these factors the level of trade is predicted. So therefore, trade doesn’t predict war but the endogenous (indepdent factors) that affect trade are said to be the cause or prevention of conflict.
Endogoeous means from within, so factors from within a country that affect it’s willingness to trade with another country or have a conflict.

Trade doens’t necessarily prevent war

Opium War, War of 1812. These wars were caused directly BY trade. When the trade is unfair or unbalanceed, the country that is disadvantaged may not be willing to continue the relationship. The weaker side may be more willing to dirupt the relationship with conflict. A stronger power may try to control a weaker country via economic coercion (sanctions).
So by this logic there is correlation between trade and peace is just as strong between trade and conflict.

title: Lecture 9-9-2026
text:
Balance of Power Theory and power-transition theory are both systemic theories, they explain war and peace with reference to the overall distribution of power across the system.



Disparty in power between major powers can make states feel insecure.
Power imbalance is treated as a paossible cause of war, and bipolarity is presented as potentially producting greater stability.
The balance-of-power tradition developed in multipolar systems where states sought to prevent the emergence of a hegemonic power.
Alliance formation is one method of balancing power.
A fundamental assumption is that states seek power because of security concerns in a self-help system.





Parity in power between major powers can create insecurity, so power balance is treated as a more probable cause of war.
Power preponderance can produce a more peacful international system, with implications at both the dyadic and systemic levels.
The direct cause of systemic instability is a shift in power between a rising challenger and a dominant status-quo power.

So in one theory (Balance of Power) two major powers with equal power creates a stable political system, whereas Power Transition Theory states that a single hegemon creates a stable system and countries rising in power create a higher likleihood of conflict.




Anarchy means the lack of a central authority capable of dictating and enforcing the legitimate use of force above sovereign states.
Anarchy does not mean chaos or complete abscense of order, international orders can and do exist.
Even realist theories recognize that mechanisms such as the balance of power can create forms of international order.
Anarchy differentiates international politics from domestic politics, where hierarchical enforcement mechanisms normally exist.





Soereignty implies that there are no de jure or de factor enforcement mechanisms reliably superior to states in all matters of security.
In a self-help system, states ultimately defend themselves through their own capabilites rather than relying completely on external protection.
Even when states would prefer mutual restrait such as complete disarmament, each state faces uncertainty about whether the other will remain commited.





A state’s attempt at self-defense may involve military build up.
Other states cannot be certain whether the increased military power is purely defensive.
Even a defensive buildup can therefore increase the security concerns of rivals or opponents.
Fear of exploitation creates a cooperation versus defection problem.
An arms race is a natural outcome of this dilemma.

title: Lecture 9-9-2026
text:
Classical Realism
Key Figures: E. H. Carr and Hans J Morenthau.

Core Assumptions

State behavior originates in power seeking human nature
International and domestic politics share the logic of power politics.
Justice, law, and morality are conditioned by power politics.
Power balancing and the distribution of power shape international outcomes.

title: Lecture 9-9-2026
section: Morgenthau’s Six Principles of Classical Realism
text:
Morgenthau’s Six Principles of Classical Realism

Politics is governed by objective laws rooted in human nature.
Interest is defined in terms of power.
Interest defined as power is unversally valid and constate, althought the meaning and forms of power may change.
The moral significance of political actions must be considered in the context of political consequences.
There is no universially agreed set of moral principals among states.
The political sphere is autonomous from legal, moral, or economic spheres, politics should be studied on it’s own terms rather than governed by legal or moral guidelines.

Kenneth Waltz

Great powers are expected to balance rather than bandwagon.

Differences from Classical Realism

title: Lecture 9-9-2026
text:
Defensive and Offensive Realism
The speaker in the video essays is John Mearsheimer, he’s an offensive realist.

Offensive Realism

Great powers seek additional power beyond minimal security.
The best route to survival is to acquire as much REGIONAL power as possible.
Great powers aspire to regional hegemony when oppurtunity exists.



Defensive Realism

States seek enough power to survive and remain secure.
Power-seeking is justified by survival and security needs.
Balancing can punish states with excessive power.

title: lecture 9-23-2026
text:
Test is 15 questions, 11 multiple choice questions, 4 short answer questions.


Sovriegnty: States can determine their own behavior and fate. Any other entity cannot dictate state’s behavior. - Internal: Governing themselves internally and having physical boundaries but not international recognition. (Taiwan) - External: Having all of internal sovriegnty but also international recognition as a state.
Ruling Concept of State Interactions, international system is anarchic. There are still rules and ideas that guide international relations but there is no enforcement mechanism. Absence of global police is the concept of anarchy with regards to international state hood. Realism, Neorealism, all accept this assumption.
The domestic system is considered hierarchical, or there is a central authority within a state.
Westphalian Treaties in 1648 (Ended 30 year war): Many scholars believe these treaties marked the end of the feudal system and entered us into the modern system that recognized State Sovreighnty, some scholars argue Congress of Vienna was that point or the US Congress declaring independence. - State Sovriegnty is largely considered the origin of the idea of state sovreignty.
Some theories use system level analysis, state, or leader.
Neoliberalism, defensive realism are system focused: These ideas argue that because of constraints applied by the system (say international system) a state acts a certain way, this is a system level analysis. Whereas if it’s regime focused, then state, or if leader, leader

Concept of Power: Melian Dialogue, Power can be defined only by material capabilities, that’s why he believed the stronger what they can, the weaker does what they must. Power can only be understood in the realm of state interaction and their relations with eachother.

Dependece of one state on antoher can create leverage, therefore, material capabilities alone cannot fully define the concept of power.

Soft Power: A state’s ability to achieve it’s desired outcomes through attractive means rather than through military or ecnomic coercion. Sometimes considered the power of image.
Balance of Power Theory: States are more likely to be peaceful and safe when they have equal power with eachother.
Power Transition Theory: States with have power parity have greater uncertainty, and uncertainty increases the liklihood of conflict. The hegemon in the system has challengers, when the challengers power is rising, once the challengers power approaches the hegemon, war is more likely to occur.
Classical Realism
States should maximize their power, norms and principals misguide state behavior, only power should guide state behavior.
Defensive Realism vs Offensive Realism:

Defensive Realism (Neorealism) the ultimate goal of state is security and survival
Offensive Realists believe states must accrue more power in order to become regional hegemon’s which secures adequate security.

Regional Hegemons tend to prevent other hegemons from rising.


How International Institutions Among States

Reducing Uncertainty
Informing States about Future Behavior
Punitive mechanisms
Reductions in Transaction Costs

Concept of Relative Gains Realists belive that states care about not only their own gains, but also gains relative to their own. If a state gains much more than my state I’m concerned. Neoliberal Institutionalists worry more about absolute gains.
Democratic Peace:

Democracies tend not to go to war with eachother.

Monatic & Diatic Democractic Peace

Democracies tend to be more peaceful overall, monatic explanation of democractic peace.

In 1992 David Lake found that democracies win more often than lose in warfighting. The major work was done by Reiter and Stam (2002) and they distinguished two clear mechanisms:
In terms of duration of wars, democracies tend to have wars of shorter lengths than that of Anoncracy and Autocracy. Democracies also tend to have lesser casualties.


In democracies political leaders tend to want to maintain their political offices, fighting a losing war is a really good way to lose your office, therefore, democratic leaders tend to choose wars they can win.
Democracies tend to initiate conflicts against targets that are inferior, as opposed to autocracies that will initiate wars against inferior targets. This is called the Selection Mechanism
When democratic leaders lose a war they are very likely to lose their office. THis mechanism is based on the selctorate theory. Democracies are not inherently better warfighters, however, they tend to select particular kinds of wars they are more likely to win.
When you compare the combatants of the above table, democratic war powers have drastically more resources and power than their opposing belligerents. Despite this, autocratic leaders tend to face harsher consequences when losing wars as the result of them losing office tends to be more severe in nature.
Democracies are more willing and more able to mobilize resources, once committed, democratic resources tend to overwhelm autocracies. When autocracies and democratic leaders started wars (in war games) with identical resources, 2/3 of the time democratic leaders outspent autocratic opponents. Reiter and Stam argue that democratic societies are more open and are able to be more innovative and have a more transparent and therefore effective communication which provides better logistics, leadership, and initiative.
Overall, democracies (democratic peace) tend to not fight against eachother. Democratic societies tend to fight harder but also tend to select wars that are easier to win. Democracies also tend to fight shorter wars. As wars drag on, democratic societies tend to lose their initiative whereas autocratic societies tend to be able to fight harder for longer. When a democratic war drags on, it may become the political high ground to stop fighting the war.
